<reason>A razor-thin call. PRO built a coherent consequentialist case (bans export demand, regulation enables protections, need ≠ coercion or every wage is coercive) and landed a genuine hit with Q2, forcing CON to concede it would not enforce hand-over. But CON did more damaging work turning PRO's own material: the screening criterion as an admission that pay recruits, "quit into what?", the pre-birth order as the openly chosen coercive horn, the factual correction that India/Thailand scandals arose in legal paid markets (PRO had blamed bans), and the sharp flip of PRO's "ongoing consent" kidney distinction. CON answered both pressure questions honestly and made the adoption-law analogy do real work in absorbing the concession. CON's case has a live weakness (its "payment is coercion" premise drifts from destitution to "households where a large sum matters," which risks proving too much, and the Ukraine "retreat to bans" claim is shaky) and its Rebuttal 2 was clipped, which keeps the margin small. Still, CON's dilemma structure and closing ("the pay recruits; the order compels") made the decisive question clearer than PRO's more list-driven regulatory promises.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>[B2.1]–[B2.7] and [B4.5]–[B4.7]: CON took PRO's own protections — screening out women in acute crisis, pre-birth parentage orders, and the "high, time-limited pay" surrogate profile — and reframed each as evidence that the market runs on financial pressure and enforces the transaction against the birth mother, turning PRO's regulatory detail into CON's dilemma.</best_rebuttal>
